claims.text: A business plan is a document containing the business objectives and important details about the operations and finance of the firm. It explains what the enterprise intends to do, for whom, how it will operate and how it expects to finance the activity. It supports coordinated decisions, communication with potential funders and later review. Forecasts are assumptions to test, not promises that sales or funding will occur. A useful plan connects its sections: planned demand must fit capacity, staffing, spending and cash timing. A polished document cannot compensate for unrealistic evidence. Review the plan when conditions change rather than treating completion of the document as completion of the business.

claims.text: A business plan includes a description of the business, market research, a marketing plan, production plan, organisational plan, financial plan and action plan. The description establishes the proposal and objectives. Research supports demand assumptions; marketing explains the target and offering; production explains how output will be supplied; organisation allocates responsibilities; finance sets out needs, sources and forecasts; the action plan turns decisions into timed tasks. These are connected components, not interchangeable names. Compare assumptions across them: a large sales target is inconsistent with too little capacity unless the plan explains how capacity will change. A production schedule alone leaves ownership, demand and finance unanswered.

claims.text: A business plan helps set goals, define the product, identify the consumer, organise research, coordinate marketing and seek finance. It can reveal gaps before money is committed and provide a reference against which actual progress is reviewed. A potential lender can assess the proposal and repayment assumptions, but a plan does not guarantee approval. Managers can assign actions and investigate differences between forecast and actual results. The plan should be updated when evidence changes: a lost customer can affect production, promotion and cash together. Uses are the decisions the document supports; elements are its contents. Explain the link rather than merely repeating a section heading.

claims.text: The organisational plan identifies roles, responsibilities, staffing and reporting. It shows who will carry out the proposed work and which skills are needed. claims.text: The financial plan identifies start-up and operating needs, finance sources, expected income and costs and cash timing. Explain assumptions and whether funding is agreed or only proposed. Profit forecasts and cash forecasts answer different questions: a credit sale can add profit before receipt. Test whether payments fall due before funds arrive. A lender assesses viability and repayment, so a document full of unsupported optimistic figures is weak evidence.

claims.text: An action plan turns the proposal into specific tasks, responsible people, deadlines and dependencies. It lets managers coordinate implementation and check progress. A deadline should allow prerequisite work: equipment cannot be tested before it is obtained and staff cannot use a process safely before relevant preparation. Review missed tasks and revise the schedule where necessary rather than record dates without follow-up.
